lessons.title: The W: how the league works
lessons.objective: Explain the WNBA season, standings and playoff format.

payload.prompt: How long is a WNBA season compared to the NBA?

options.text: 44 games in 2026, growing to 50-52 in later years; NBA has 82 games.
WNBA plays 82 games like the NBA.
WNBA seasons are only 30 games, much shorter.

explanation.correct: Right. The WNBA plays 44 games in 2026 (up from 40), and the 2026 CBA phases in 50 games by 2027-28 and 52 by 2029-32.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The WNBA plays 44 games in 2026 as part of the new CBA growth schedule.

payload.prompt: What format does the WNBA playoffs use?

options.text: Best-of-three first round, best-of-five semifinals, best-of-seven Finals.
Best-of-seven in all rounds, like the NBA.
Single-elimination tournament.

explanation.correct: Right. The WNBA uses best-of-three to start (quick eliminations), best-of-five in the middle rounds, then best-of-seven Finals.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The WNBA uses best-of-three first round, best-of-five next, then best-of-seven Finals.

payload.prompt: Order the WNBA season by month (2026).

explanation.correct: The season flows: regular play, mid-season Cup, then playoffs.
explanation.incorrect: The WNBA runs May–September for regular season, with Commissioner's Cup mid-season and playoffs in late September.

payload.prompt: The Commissioner's Cup is a mid-season WNBA tournament like the {{blank}} in the NBA.
payload.template: The Commissioner's Cup is a mid-season WNBA tournament like the {{gap1}} in the NBA.

explanation.correct: The Cup is the WNBA's in-season tournament, matching the NBA Cup format.
explanation.incorrect: The Commissioner's Cup mirrors the NBA Cup, a mid-season tournament.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: The W season is so short. The NBA plays like 82 games.

payload.question: What is she noticing?

options.text: She is comparing the WNBA's shorter schedule (44 games in 2026) to the NBA's 82 games.
The WNBA does not have playoffs.
The WNBA season is only one month long.
WNBA games are shorter than NBA games.

payload.translation: WNBA plays 44 games in 2026 vs NBA's 82. The CBA grows it to 50, then 52. Shorter by design.

followUps.line: Yeah, but they play such intense basketball. Quality over quantity.
followUps.why: You acknowledge her point and reframe it positively.

followUps.line: Do you think more games would make it better or worse?
followUps.why: You turn it into a question about her preference.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: The WNBA schedule is shorter by design; it is not a weakness. Respect the league's choice.

lessons.title: WNBA rules and ball differences
lessons.objective: Compare WNBA and NBA on quarters, ball and three-point line.

pairs.definition: WNBA: four 10-minute quarters (40 minutes total). NBA: four 12-minute quarters (48 minutes).
WNBA: 22 ft 1.75 in. NBA: 23 ft 9 in at the top (22 ft in corners).
Both: 24 seconds, same resets on offensive rebounds (24 in WNBA, 14 in NBA).

distractorDefinitions: WNBA has 5 fouls per player; NBA has 6.
WNBA games are 60 minutes; NBA games are 48 minutes.

explanation.summary: The WNBA plays quarters (not halves) with a shorter game clock, a closer three-point line, and the same shot clock as the NBA.

payload.prompt: The WNBA ball is smaller than the NBA ball. True?

choices.label: False, they use the same size.

explanation.correct: Right. The WNBA ball is 28.5 inches; the NBA ball is 29.5 inches. A slightly smaller ball is standard for the women's game.
explanation.incorrect: Actually, the WNBA uses a 28.5-inch ball; the NBA uses 29.5 inches. The smaller ball reflects hand size differences and is standard across women's leagues.

payload.prompt: The WNBA three-point line is farther from the basket than the NBA line. True?

scene.alt: WNBA and NBA three-point line distance.

choices.label: False, WNBA is closer (22 ft 1.75 in).

explanation.correct: Right. The WNBA three-point line (22 ft 1.75 in) is closer than the NBA's (23 ft 9 in at the top). A closer line is also standard in women's leagues.
explanation.incorrect: Actually, the WNBA line is closer: 22 ft 1.75 in vs NBA's 23 ft 9 in at the top. This reflects the women's game conventions.

payload.prompt: How do WNBA and NBA game lengths compare?

options.text: WNBA: 40 minutes in four 10-minute quarters. NBA: 48 minutes in four 12-minute quarters.
Both are 48 minutes; WNBA also uses quarters.
WNBA is 36 minutes; NBA is 48 minutes.

explanation.correct: Exactly. WNBA games are 40 minutes in regulation, eight minutes shorter than the NBA's 48.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. WNBA plays 40 minutes (four 10-minute quarters); NBA plays 48 minutes (four 12-minute quarters).

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: The ball is smaller in the W. That makes sense, right?

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: She is noting that the WNBA ball (28.5 in) is smaller than the NBA ball (29.5 in).
The W uses a bigger ball than the NBA.
Ball size determines who wins.
WNBA players prefer light balls.

payload.translation: Smaller ball is standard in women's basketball (28.5 in vs NBA 29.5 in). It's normal, not a weakness.

followUps.line: It's practical. Does ball size change how they shoot?
followUps.why: You validate her observation and ask a thoughtful follow-up.

followUps.line: Yeah, same reason college women and international use smaller balls.
followUps.why: You connect it to a broader standard, showing you understand women's basketball culture.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Smaller ball is not inferior; it is standard in women's basketball globally.

lessons.title: The CBA and the money
lessons.objective: Explain the 2026 CBA, the cap and why it was a big deal.

payload.prompt: What is the WNBA salary cap for 2026?

options.text: About $7.0 million; first-year max salary around $1.4 million.
About $50 million, similar to the NBA.
There is no salary cap in the WNBA.

explanation.correct: Right. The 2026 WNBA cap is about $7.0 million per team. A first-year maximum salary is around $1.4 million, much less than NBA stars.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The WNBA cap is about $7.0 million, with first-year max around $1.4 million, far below the NBA's.

payload.prompt: What is the roster size for WNBA teams?

options.text: 12 players on active roster plus 2 developmental spots (14 total).
15 players, like the NBA.
8 players, very small rosters.

explanation.correct: Right. The new CBA set rosters at 12 plus 2 developmental spots, giving teams 14 total. Developmental players can move up.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The 2026 CBA specifies 12 roster players plus 2 developmental spots.

payload.prompt: WNBA cap as % of NBA cap (2026)?

explanation.correct: Close. WNBA ~$7M is about 4–5% of NBA ~$155M. Gap is shrinking.
explanation.incorrect: WNBA cap is 4–5% of NBA. New media deals (ESPN, Amazon Prime) are raising salaries.

explanation.correct: Right. CBA: 44 games 2026, rising to 50 by 2027–28, then 52 by 2029.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: WNBA players make so much less than NBA players. That seems unfair.

payload.question: What is she raising?

options.text: A fairness concern: WNBA salaries (cap ~$7M) are much lower than NBA (cap ~$155M).
WNBA players do not have a salary cap.
NBA players are not paid at all.
The WNBA has no revenue.

payload.translation: Pay gap is real. 2026 CBA was a win: $1.4M max (up from $250K), 44 games, cap grows. New media deals (ESPN, Amazon Prime) are closing the gap.

followUps.line: The new CBA was a big raise. Did you hear about the media deals?
followUps.why: You acknowledge her fairness concern and introduce the progress made.

followUps.line: What do you think would close the gap faster?
followUps.why: You invite her perspective on solutions.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: The pay gap is real and worth talking about. The 2026 CBA was a historic win for WNBA players and is closing it year by year.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: I read that the WNBA just signed a huge TV deal. Is that why salaries jumped?

payload.question: What is she connecting?

options.text: She is linking the new media deals (ESPN, Amazon Prime) to the salary increases in the 2026 CBA.
WNBA players do not benefit from TV deals.
Media deals only help the NBA.
The salary increase was unrelated to TV money.

payload.translation: Exactly. 2026 CBA + new media partnerships (ESPN, Amazon Prime) bring more revenue = higher salary cap. TV deals drive player pay.

followUps.line: So the TV deal was the reason for the raise?
followUps.why: You dig into her connection and confirm it respectfully.

followUps.line: Are you watching the W more because of the exposure?
followUps.why: You turn it into a conversation about her fandom and media growth.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Media deals and player revenue sharing are directly connected. The WNBA's new TV partnerships are a game-changer for salaries.

lessons.title: Draft, expansion and where players play
lessons.objective: Explain expansion drafts, the draft and offseason leagues.

payload.prompt: What happened in the 2026 WNBA expansion draft?

options.text: Toronto Tempo and Portland Fire joined; existing teams exposed players; new teams drafted 23 players each.
No new teams joined in 2026.
All existing teams lost their rosters in the draft.

explanation.correct: Right. Toronto and Portland expanded into the WNBA in 2026 via an expansion draft on April 3, 2026. Each team drafted 23 players from existing rosters.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. In 2026, Toronto Tempo and Portland Fire joined via expansion draft (April 3, 2026), selecting players from existing teams.

payload.prompt: When does the WNBA draft happen?

options.text: Early April, before the season. College seniors and international players are eligible.
In June, after the NBA draft.
In January, mid-season.

explanation.correct: Right. The WNBA draft is in early April, picking from college seniors and eligible international players. It happens before the regular season.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The WNBA draft is in April, selecting from college players ready to turn pro and international talent.

items.text: Players play overseas or in offseason leagues (winter/spring)

explanation.correct: Players often play overseas in winter/spring for income and competition.
explanation.incorrect: WNBA's calendar: season ends October, overseas play November–March, draft April, season starts May.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: She plays in the W but also overseas in the winter. Does she get a break?

payload.question: What is she wondering?

options.text: She is asking if WNBA players play year-round (WNBA May–Oct, plus overseas in winter).
WNBA players do not play overseas.
Overseas leagues are only for injured players.
Players must sit out every other year.

payload.translation: Many WNBA stars play overseas (Europe, China) Nov–March for income. Calendar: May–Oct WNBA, Nov–Mar overseas, April draft.

followUps.line: That sounds intense. Do they get paid differently overseas?
followUps.why: You show curiosity about her economics and player compensation.

followUps.line: So the W season is only half the year for her?
followUps.why: You summarize it in a way that shows you understand the schedule.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Overseas play is normal for WNBA players. It is additional income and competition; the WNBA season is only part of their professional calendar.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: Toronto and Portland got new teams! Are they going to be good right away?

payload.question: What is she asking?

options.text: She is curious if expansion teams (Tempo, Fire) can compete immediately after the expansion draft.
Toronto and Portland will definitely win the championship.
Expansion teams can never win.
The draft has no effect on team quality.

payload.translation: Expansion teams draft from existing rosters (23 players each), so both Tempo and Fire get talent immediately. But building chemistry takes time.

followUps.line: So they might sneak into the playoffs?
followUps.why: You explore the possibility she raised.

followUps.line: Which one are you rooting for?
followUps.why: You invite her fandom into the conversation.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Expansion teams can compete immediately because they draft from existing rosters. Toronto and Portland both got solid talent pools.

lessons.title: From campus to the W
lessons.objective: Follow a college star's path to the pros.

payload.prompt: What is the usual path for a college player to the WNBA?

options.text: Declare for the April WNBA draft after college; get drafted by a team; sign rookie contract.
Play in college and get a direct free-agent offer from a WNBA team.
WNBA teams recruit directly from high school.

explanation.correct: Right. College players declare for the WNBA draft in April, teams select them, and they sign rookie contracts. Some go undrafted and sign as free agents.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The standard path is college → declare for draft → drafted by a WNBA team → rookie contract.

payload.prompt: What is a rookie contract in the WNBA?

options.text: First professional contract; length and salary set by draft position (first pick gets max, later rounds get less).
A deal that lasts a player's entire career.
Rookies sign with overseas leagues first.

explanation.correct: Right. WNBA rookie contracts are standardized: first overall picks get the highest salary (first-year max ~$1.4M), and later picks get progressively less.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Rookie contracts are first-time pro deals with salary tied to draft position.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: She was the number one pick! Do you think she'll be a star or bust?

payload.question: What is she wondering?

options.text: She is asking whether a top draft pick will succeed in the WNBA or underperform.
She thinks number one picks always become superstars.
The draft determines a player's entire career.
High picks never succeed.

payload.translation: #1 picks get elite talent, ~$1.4M salary, high expectations. But pro jump is huge. Some become MVPs; others develop slowly.

followUps.line: What would count as a good rookie year for her?
followUps.why: You ask her standard for success, not assuming it.

followUps.line: Has she had a chance to play much yet?
followUps.why: You ground it in her actual season performance.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: No pick is a sure thing. College dominance doesn't guarantee pro success. Respect the unknown.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: The rookies make so little compared to stars. That doesn't seem fair.

payload.question: What is she pointing out?

options.text: She is noting the salary gap between rookie contracts (~$1.4M for #1 pick) and veteran stars.
All WNBA players earn the same salary.
Rookies make more than veterans.
Salary is not based on experience.

payload.translation: Rookies make less than stars. #1 max is $1.4M; vets earn more. Seniority pays off in every league.

followUps.line: Do rookies get raises if they play well?
followUps.why: You ask about performance bonuses and career trajectory.

followUps.line: How long before she could become one of the top earners?
followUps.why: You show interest in her long-term projection.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Rookies earn less because they are unproven. As they gain experience and win awards, salaries rise. This is standard in sports.

payload.title: College star to the W
payload.setting: She just said a college star you both like declared for the WNBA draft. How do you chat?

exchanges.theirMessage: I hope she goes to a good team. I'd love to see her stay close to home.

replies.text: That would be cool. Do you think she'll go early in the draft?
replies.theirResponse: She should. She's one of the best in her class.
replies.coachNote: Good. You respected her wish and asked about draft odds, showing engagement.

replies.text: Yeah, but draft order is the hard part. She doesn't get to pick.
replies.theirResponse: True. I just hope she lands somewhere with a chance to play.
replies.coachNote: Perfect. You acknowledged the reality that players don't control draft outcomes, and she refined her hope. Great conversation.

replies.text: Home team or not, she'll make it anywhere.
replies.theirResponse: I guess, but it matters to fans.
replies.coachNote: You dismissed her feeling instead of engaging with why location matters to her as a fan. Next time explore her preference.

payload.closingNote: Draft outcomes are uncertain, but a player's long-term arc is what matters. Be curious about where she wants to land and why it matters to her.

payload.title: Rookie salaries talk
payload.setting: She is surprised by how much rookies make (or don't). How do you put it in context?

exchanges.theirMessage: I looked up a rookie contract and was shocked. That doesn't seem like enough to live on.

replies.text: Yeah, $1.4 million for the #1 pick sounds like a lot but it has to cover life and taxes.
replies.theirResponse: Right, and that's the maximum. Later picks make less.
replies.coachNote: Good. You grounded it in reality (taxes, living costs) without dismissing her surprise.

replies.text: It's way less than NBA rookies, but the WNBA cap is much smaller right now.
replies.theirResponse: So the league's revenue determines salaries?
replies.coachNote: Excellent. You explained the constraint, and she asked a follow-up. You've opened her thinking about league economics.

replies.text: That's plenty of money. Athletes shouldn't complain.
replies.theirResponse: Well, it's their career and their income.
replies.coachNote: You shut down her curiosity instead of exploring her concern. Next time honor the economic reality players face.

payload.closingNote: Rookie salaries reflect both opportunity and constraint. Respect that income needs are real; future earnings depend on performance and league growth.

lessons.title: Following {{team}} in the W
lessons.objective: Follow {{team}} across the season and its playoff race.

payload.prompt: How many WNBA teams make the playoffs?

options.text: Eight teams (four per conference) for the first round; format depends on standings and play-in considerations.
Four teams total.
All 12 teams make the playoffs.

explanation.correct: Right. Eight WNBA teams make playoffs: the top seeds in each conference, plus teams competing for play-in spots if needed. With 12 teams total (after 2026 expansion), the playoff field is roughly top 8.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Eight teams make the WNBA playoffs out of 12 total. The exact format depends on standings.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: They are still fighting for a playoff spot! The season is almost over.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: She is noting that her team is in a close race for one of the eight playoff positions late in the season.
Her team has already clinched the playoff spot.
The WNBA playoffs happen in May.
Only one team makes the playoffs.

payload.translation: She is right to worry. With the WNBA regular season ending in late September and playoffs starting September 27 (2026), late-season games decide which eight teams advance. A team fighting for a spot is in a tense stretch; wins and losses matter. That is the drama that hooks fans.

followUps.line: Do they have any must-win games left?
followUps.why: You engage with the urgency she is feeling.

followUps.line: What do they need to do to make it?
followUps.why: You ask her analysis, not assuming you know.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Playoff races are intense. Show interest in her team's pressure and remaining path.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: She just got hurt. I'm so worried she won't be back for the playoffs.

payload.question: What is she worried about?

options.text: She is concerned that an injury to a key player might sideline them for the playoffs.
All injuries automatically mean a player misses the season.
Injuries do not affect playoff teams.
She thinks the playoffs are only for healthy teams.

payload.translation: Late-season injuries can derail playoff hopes. Recovery varies: weeks to surgery. Her worry is legitimate.

followUps.line: Do you know how long she's out?
followUps.why: You ask for specifics, not assumptions.

followUps.line: Can the team still make it without her?
followUps.why: You explore whether there is still a path forward.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Late-season injuries are devastating to playoff hopes. Respect her concern; injuries matter.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: We made it! We are in the playoffs!

payload.question: What is she celebrating?

options.text: Her team has clinched one of the eight playoff spots.
Her team won the championship.
The team got drafted into the WNBA.
Her team secured a home game in the first round.

payload.translation: That is a huge moment for her and the team. Making the playoffs means eight weeks of basketball (September 27 through October playoffs), starting with best-of-three series. First-round elimination is harsh, but at least they got in. Celebrate this with her; it is real progress.

followUps.line: Who is your first-round matchup?
followUps.why: You show enthusiasm about the upcoming series.

followUps.line: Do you think you can make a run?
followUps.why: You invite her to dream big about their playoff chances.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Making the playoffs is a milestone. Share her joy, and ask about their playoff path.

payload.title: Playoffs are coming
payload.setting: Her WNBA team is in the playoff race. How do you talk about their chances?

exchanges.theirMessage: I'm so nervous. If we don't make it, the season is over.

replies.text: The W playoffs are intense. One loss and you're out in the first round.
replies.theirResponse: Exactly. I can't handle the stress.
replies.coachNote: Good. You acknowledged the intensity of best-of-three series without being dismissive of her anxiety.

replies.text: But your team has been playing great. You could sneak out of the first round.
replies.theirResponse: That's true. We've won four straight. I feel better.
replies.coachNote: Perfect. You grounded her worry in their actual recent performance and gave her reason to hope.

replies.text: It's not that big a deal. It's just basketball.
replies.coachNote: Ouch. You dismissed the thing she cares about. Next time honor her investment in the team, even if you don't share it.

payload.closingNote: Playoff races are stressful for fans. Validate the tension, ask about their team's odds, and be hopeful together.

payload.title: After the playoff game
payload.setting: Her team just won (or lost) a playoff game. How do you respond?

exchanges.theirMessage: We just beat them! That was so close, but we're moving on!

replies.text: That game was insane. Who played the best for you?
replies.theirResponse: Number 24 had 28 points in the second half. She saved us.
replies.coachNote: Excellent. You asked for specifics and let her relive her team's heroics. She got to share the victory.

replies.text: Congrats! You guys are moving on!
replies.theirResponse: Thanks! Now we wait for the next matchup.
replies.coachNote: Good, but generic. You could have asked who stood out or what happens next to deepen the connection.

replies.text: Cool, but you'll probably get crushed in the next round.
replies.coachNote: Ouch. You killed her joy instead of celebrating. Never predict defeat; let her enjoy the win.

payload.closingNote: Playoff wins are huge. Celebrate with her, ask about standout players, and build excitement for the next round.
